title: Intel Shares Dip as TSMC Targets Elon Musk’s Terafab Venture, Sparking Market Shock
body:
Intel’s shares slumped on Tuesday after the company’s flagship Texas fab project—dubbed “Terafab”—caught the eye of a new heavyweight contender: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC). The development was confirmed by Elon Musk, who said TSMC is evaluating participation in the $30‑billion venture that Intel originally announced in April. The prospect of a rival chipmaker joining the project has sparked concerns among investors that Intel’s first‑of‑its‑kind effort to rebuild U.S. manufacturing capacity could be diluted, prompting a sharp sell‑off in the chipmaker’s stock.

The Terafab initiative, slated to be built near Austin, Texas, is intended to restore a domestic supply chain for advanced logic chips and to counter growing geopolitical pressures on the semiconductor industry. Intel pledged to invest $30 billion in a 2,000‑acre campus that would house multiple 300‑millimetre wafer fabs capable of producing 5‑nanometre and later 3‑nanometre nodes. The project is also central to the U.S. government’s “CHIPS for America” agenda, which offers subsidies and tax incentives to firms that locate high‑tech manufacturing on U.S. soil. By securing a partnership with TSMC, Intel hoped to accelerate the timeline, share risk, and attract additional talent to the region.

Musk’s confirmation that TSMC is “talking” about joining the Texas venture sent a jolt through the market. While Intel’s board has not yet disclosed any formal agreement, the mere possibility of a direct competitor sharing the same site raises strategic questions. TSMC, the world’s largest pure‑play foundry, commands a dominant share of the global advanced‑node market, supplying Apple, Nvidia and many other fabless designers. If the Taiwanese giant were to co‑locate with Intel, the two could potentially collaborate on tooling, supply chains and workforce development, but they could also end up competing for the same customers and government incentives.

Analysts at several Wall Street firms flagged the news as a “double‑edged sword.” On one hand, a joint Texas hub could create a semiconductor ecosystem rivaling the scale of Silicon Valley, driving down costs for both companies and reinforcing the United States’ strategic autonomy. On the other hand, investors worry that Intel’s equity stake in the project could be diluted, and that any profit‑sharing arrangement might erode the margins Intel expects from its own fab output. The stock reaction reflects these mixed sentiments: Intel fell roughly 4 percent in after‑hours trading, wiping out nearly $12 billion in market value, while TSMC’s shares in Hong Kong edged higher on speculation that the partnership could open a new revenue stream beyond its traditional foundry model.

Beyond the immediate market impact, the development underscores a broader shift in the semiconductor landscape. The United States has been courting foreign manufacturers to bolster its domestic capacity, offering billions in subsidies through the CHIPS Act. TSMC’s potential entry into Texas signals that the policy is bearing fruit, encouraging even its biggest rivals to consider a foothold in the country. However, the move also raises regulatory and security considerations, as U.S. officials weigh the benefits of foreign investment against concerns over intellectual property and supply‑chain resilience.

Looking ahead, the next few weeks will be crucial. Intel is expected to host a briefing with the Department of Commerce and the White House to outline the partnership framework, while TSMC is likely to conduct a detailed feasibility study before committing capital. If the two firms can forge a clear, mutually beneficial agreement, the Texas Terafab could become a landmark of cross‑border cooperation, accelerating the rollout of next‑generation chips for AI, automotive and data‑center applications. Conversely, a failure to align interests could stall the project, leaving Intel to shoulder the full financial burden and potentially weakening the United States’ strategic position in the global chip race. The outcome will shape not only Intel’s stock trajectory but also the broader narrative of how the world rebuilds its semiconductor supply chain in the post‑pandemic era.
